title: Political Discourse
subtitle: Master the rhetoric, debate format and crisis language of French political life

lessons.title: L'art du discours politique
lessons.description: Mastery-level rhetorical technique in political speech: the classical appeals, compression devices and strategic evasions, analysed on invented Valdonian speeches.

blocks.heading: Ethos, pathos, logos : les trois appuis du discours politique
blocks.body: Classical rhetoric names three levers of persuasion, and political speech rarely uses only one. L'ethos is the credibility the speaker claims by virtue of who they are or what they have lived through. Le pathos moves the audience through emotion — fear, pride, indignation. Le logos appeals to reasoning: figures, causal chains, precedents. A mastery-level speech braids the three so that the audience feels it is being reasoned with, even when logos is the thinnest of the three strands. Your job as analyst is to weigh the proportions, not just spot the labels.

examples.french: En tant qu'ancien maire de Bellerive, je connais le prix du béton et celui du silence.
examples.english: As a former mayor of Bellerive, I know the cost of concrete and the cost of silence.
examples.note: Invented line: ethos (the mayoral past) fused with a rhetorical image.

examples.french: Songez à cet enfant qui attend le bus sous la pluie depuis six ans.
examples.english: Think of that child who has waited for the bus in the rain for six years.
examples.note: Pathos: a single, unverifiable but vivid case stands in for a policy failure.

examples.french: Trois hôpitaux fermés, deux cents lits perdus : les chiffres parlent d'eux-mêmes.
examples.english: Three hospitals closed, two hundred beds lost: the figures speak for themselves.
examples.note: Logos, though the causal claim behind the figures is left unstated.

examples.french: Un discours équilibré ne choisit pas entre les trois appuis, il les dose.
examples.english: A well-balanced speech does not choose between the three supports, it proportions them.

examples.french: Repérer lequel des trois domine, c'est déjà comprendre la stratégie de l'orateur.
examples.english: Spotting which of the three dominates already tells you the speaker's strategy.

blocks.tip: In commentary, name the dominant appeal first: « ce passage relève avant tout du pathos », then show how the other two are used to disguise that imbalance.

blocks.heading: Le kairos : le moment qui fait le discours
blocks.body: Le kairos is the opportune moment — the sense that a phrase lands because of when it is spoken, not only what it says. A mastery-level speaker reads the room: a pause after bad news, a rise in volume right after the opponent's weakest point, silence held one second past comfort. Kairos cannot be quoted in a transcript, which is exactly why it is powerful and why analysts often underrate it. When you read a speech on the page, you must reconstruct the missing kairos from stage directions, applause markers and the surrounding events.

examples.french: Il a attendu que les huées s'éteignent avant de reprendre, plus bas.
examples.english: He waited for the jeering to die down before continuing, more quietly.
examples.note: Kairos as timing: the pause itself is the rhetorical move.

examples.french: Le bon mot n'existe que rapporté au moment exact où il tombe.
examples.english: The right phrase only exists in relation to the exact moment it lands.

examples.french: Prononcée la veille, la même phrase serait passée inaperçue.
examples.english: Spoken the day before, the same sentence would have gone unnoticed.

examples.french: Le kairos se prépare : l'improvisation apparente est souvent minutée.
examples.english: Kairos is prepared: the apparent spontaneity is often timed to the second.

examples.french: Sur transcription seule, le kairos disparaît ; il faut relire le contexte.
examples.english: On the transcript alone, kairos disappears; you have to reread the context.

blocks.heading: La prétérition : dire en prétendant ne pas dire
blocks.body: La prétérition announces that a subject will not be raised — and raises it anyway, with the added benefit of sounding restrained. « Je ne dirai pas que mon adversaire a menti » plants the accusation while letting the speaker claim they never made it. It is one of the most efficient devices in political French because it delivers the content of an attack while keeping the deniability of a refusal. Pair it, when you analyse, with la dénégation — the parallel move of denying something while performing the very thing denied.

examples.french: Je ne rappellerai pas les promesses non tenues du dernier mandat.
examples.english: I will not bring up the broken promises of the last term.
examples.note: Prétérition: the attack is delivered inside the refusal to deliver it.

examples.french: Loin de moi l'idée de parler d'incompétence.
examples.english: Far be it from me to speak of incompetence.
examples.note: A classic frame: the disclaimer and the accusation share one sentence.

examples.french: Je ne suis pas venu pour attaquer, mais pour comparer les bilans.
examples.english: I have not come to attack, but to compare the records.

examples.french: La prétérition offre le contenu d'une charge sans la responsabilité d'une charge.
examples.english: Praeteritio delivers the content of an attack without the responsibility of one.

examples.french: « Ce n'est pas moi qui le dis » précède presque toujours ce qu'on ne voulait pas dire soi-même.
examples.english: "It's not me saying it" almost always precedes what the speaker did not want to say themselves.

blocks.tip: Test any prétérition by deleting the disclaimer clause. If the remaining sentence is a straightforward accusation, the disclaimer was decorative, not sincere.

blocks.heading: Le subjonctif dans le discours d'autorité
blocks.body: Political French leans on the subjunctive to sound both categorical and impersonal at once: il est impératif que, il importe que, il n'est pas exclu que, quoi qu'on en dise. The mood signals that the speaker is stating a necessity or a possibility rather than a bare fact, which lets the sentence sound principled even when it commits to nothing measurable. Note the concessive quoi que + subjonctif (quoi qu'on en dise, quoi qu'il en coûte): it pre-empts objections by conceding them in advance, inside a single clause.

examples.french: Il est impératif que cette réforme aboutisse avant l'été.
examples.english: It is imperative that this reform succeed before the summer.
examples.note: Necessity, not a promise — no one is named as responsible.

examples.french: Il importe que chacun prenne la mesure de l'enjeu.
examples.english: It is important that everyone grasp the scale of the issue.

examples.french: Quoi qu'on en dise, les résultats sont là.
examples.english: Whatever people may say, the results are there.
examples.note: Concession folded into one clause: the objection is granted and dismissed at once.

examples.french: Quoi qu'il en coûte, nous tiendrons cet engagement.
examples.english: Whatever it costs, we will keep this commitment.

examples.french: Il n'est pas exclu que le calendrier soit révisé.
examples.english: It is not ruled out that the timetable will be revised.
examples.note: A hedge dressed as a principled statement.

examples.french: Le subjonctif d'autorité affirme une nécessité sans jamais désigner qui doit agir.
examples.english: The subjunctive of authority states a necessity without ever naming who must act.

blocks.tip: Whenever you meet il est + adjective + que, ask what the sentence would lose if you deleted the adjective. Often: nothing measurable.

blocks.heading: La négation stylistique et la litote grammaticale
blocks.body: Litotes is built on grammar, not just vocabulary: ne pas être sans + noun, ce n'est pas rien, je ne dirai pas que + indicatif all say less in order to mean more. A related structure, ne pas nier que, hovers between mood: with the indicative it half-concedes the fact; with the subjunctive it keeps the fact in the realm of doubt. Mastery-level readers track which mood follows nier and treat the choice itself as a piece of evidence about how much the speaker is actually conceding.

examples.french: Ce dossier n'est pas sans poser quelques difficultés.
examples.english: This matter is not without posing a few difficulties.
examples.note: Litotes: a serious problem, minimised by double negation.

examples.french: Je ne dirai pas que la situation est simple.
examples.english: I will not say the situation is simple.
examples.note: Understatement standing in for "it is genuinely difficult".

examples.french: On ne peut nier que les délais ont été dépassés.
examples.english: It cannot be denied that the deadlines were missed.
examples.note: Indicative after « nier » here: the fact is effectively conceded.

examples.french: Je ne nie pas qu'il y ait eu des erreurs, sans plus de précision.
examples.english: I do not deny that there may have been mistakes, with no further detail.
examples.note: Subjonctif: the fact stays hypothetical, not admitted outright.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas rien, ce que nous avons obtenu cette année.
examples.english: It's not nothing, what we achieved this year.

examples.french: La litote grammaticale protège l'orateur : elle dit assez pour informer, trop peu pour engager.
examples.english: Grammatical litotes protects the speaker: it says enough to inform, too little to commit.

blocks.tip: After « nier que » and similar verbs, check the mood before you check the vocabulary — indicative concedes more than subjonctif, whatever the surrounding words claim.

passages.title: Anatomie d'une petite phrase (texte entièrement fictif)
passages.french:
Le 14 mars, à Sormont, Camille Lorrain a prononcé le discours le plus commenté de sa campagne — un texte entièrement fictif, comme l'ensemble de cette leçon.
Elle commence par une phrase d'ethos : « Fille d'ouvrière, j'ai grandi à trois arrêts de bus de cette tribune. »
L'auditoire, venu nombreux, retient son souffle avant même le premier chiffre.
Vient ensuite une prétérition soigneusement construite : « Je ne rappellerai pas les six années de silence de mon adversaire. »
Le silence, précisément, est ce qu'elle vient de rappeler, avec un aplomb tranquille.
Le chiasme qui suit fait le tour des rédactions dès le lendemain matin : « On ne bâtit pas un pays sur des promesses, on ne tient pas des promesses sans bâtir. »
C'est la petite phrase de la soirée ; elle sera citée plus souvent que le reste du discours réuni.
Le pathos arrive enfin, par une image unique : un enfant qui attend le bus sous la pluie depuis six ans.
Personne, dans la salle, ne vérifie la date ni le prénom de cet enfant ; personne n'en a besoin.
Le logos, lui, tient en une phrase : trois hôpitaux fermés, deux cents lits perdus.
Aucun chiffre n'est sourcé, mais la cadence de la phrase suffit à lui donner un poids de preuve.
Le moment le plus étudié reste le kairos final : une pause de quatre secondes avant le mot « ensemble ».
Quatre secondes, à la tribune, sont une éternité ; la salle les a comblées d'applaudissements avant même le mot.
Analyser ce discours n'est pas juger Camille Lorrain : c'est décrire une mécanique qu'elle partage avec tous ses rivaux, Adrien Fabre compris.
Le kairos, l'ethos et la prétérition ne prouvent rien ; ils rendent une position plus confortable à occuper.
C'est précisément cette différence — entre convaincre et rendre confortable — que l'analyste doit garder à l'esprit.
passages.english:
On March 14th, in Sormont, Camille Lorrain delivered the most talked-about speech of her campaign — an entirely fictional text, like the whole of this lesson.
She opens with a line of ethos: "A worker's daughter, I grew up three bus stops from this rostrum."
The audience, out in force, holds its breath before the first figure has even arrived.
Then comes a carefully built praeteritio: "I will not bring up my opponent's six years of silence."
The silence is precisely what she has just brought up, with a calm self-assurance.
The chiasmus that follows makes the rounds of every newsroom the next morning: "You do not build a country on promises, you do not keep promises without building."
It is the soundbite of the evening; it will be quoted more often than the rest of the speech combined.
Pathos arrives last, through a single image: a child who has waited for the bus in the rain for six years.
No one in the hall checks the date or the child's name; no one needs to.
Logos, for its part, fits into one sentence: three hospitals closed, two hundred beds lost.
No figure is sourced, but the cadence of the sentence is enough to give it the weight of proof.
The most studied moment remains the final kairos: a four-second pause before the word "together".
Four seconds, at the rostrum, is an eternity; the hall filled them with applause before the word even arrived.
Analysing this speech is not judging Camille Lorrain: it is describing a mechanism she shares with all her rivals, Adrien Fabre included.
Kairos, ethos and praeteritio prove nothing; they make a position more comfortable to hold.
It is precisely that difference — between persuading and making comfortable — that the analyst must keep in mind.

lessons.title: Le débat présidentiel
lessons.description: The genre conventions of the televised presidential debate: its formal structure, its register, and the techniques of control that operate within strict time limits.

blocks.heading: Le format : temps de parole, contradicteur, modérateur
blocks.body: The presidential debate is a genre with fixed rules before it is a contest of ideas. Le temps de parole is allotted and timed to the second; le modérateur (or la modératrice) enforces it and reframes questions that were dodged; le contradicteur is not an enemy in the everyday sense but a structural role — the person the format requires you to answer. Mastery-level French recognises that the genre itself shapes the language: sentences are shorter than in a rally speech, because a long sentence risks being cut off by the clock, not by an interruption.

examples.french: Madame Lorrain, il vous reste quarante-cinq secondes.
examples.english: Ms Lorrain, you have forty-five seconds left.
examples.note: Invented moderator line: the clock is a character in the genre.

examples.french: Je repose la question à monsieur Fabre, qui ne m'a pas répondu.
examples.english: I am putting the question back to Mr Fabre, who did not answer me.
examples.note: The moderator's job includes naming an evasion out loud.

examples.french: Le contradicteur n'est pas un ennemi : c'est un rôle que le format impose.
examples.english: The opposing speaker is not an enemy: it is a role the format imposes.

blocks.heading: Contrôler l'échange : esquiver, garder la main, reprendre la main
blocks.body: Because time is scarce, debate technique is largely about control rather than content. Botter en touche dodges a question by answering an adjacent one. Noyer le poisson buries a precise question under a flood of loosely related detail. Garder la main means holding the initiative — setting the terms the other side must respond to — while reprendre la main names the moment a candidate who had lost that initiative takes it back, often with a single well-aimed question or fact.

examples.french: Vous bottez en touche depuis dix minutes ; répondez sur le fond.
examples.english: You have been dodging the question for ten minutes; answer on the substance.
examples.note: The moderator naming the technique out loud, live.

examples.french: Il a noyé le poisson en citant six réformes sans lien direct avec la question.
examples.english: He muddied the waters by citing six reforms with no direct link to the question.

examples.french: Elle a gardé la main tout le premier quart d'heure, sans jamais élever la voix.
examples.english: She kept control for the whole first quarter of an hour, without ever raising her voice.

examples.french: Un seul chiffre lui a permis de reprendre la main sur la question du logement.

blocks.heading: Le registre : de la réplique posée à la punchline
blocks.body: A debate moves between two registers within the same minute. La réplique — the measured retort — belongs to the formal register of policy exchange, built on complete clauses and controlled connectors. La punchline (a loanword now standard in French political journalism) belongs to a punchier register: short, rhythmic, built to survive being clipped for the evening news. Mastery is knowing when to shift: a candidate who only produces punchlines looks evasive, one who never produces one looks unmemorable.

examples.french: Sa réplique, en trois phrases nettes, a réorienté tout l'échange.
examples.english: Her retort, in three clean sentences, redirected the whole exchange.

examples.french: « Des chiffres, pas des slogans » : la punchline de la soirée, reprise sur tous les plateaux le lendemain.
examples.english: "Figures, not slogans": the soundbite of the night, repeated on every set the next day.

examples.french: La formule choc fonctionne hors contexte ; la réplique, elle, a besoin de l'échange qui la précède.
examples.english: The punchy formula works out of context; the retort needs the exchange that precedes it.

examples.french: On reconnaît une bonne répartie à sa rapidité, pas à sa longueur.
examples.english: A good comeback is judged by its speed, not its length.

examples.french: Passer sans transition du registre soutenu à la punchline crée un effet de rupture calculé.
examples.english: Shifting without transition from formal register to a punchline creates a calculated effect of rupture.

blocks.tip: In your own commentary, distinguish « il a une bonne réplique » (a strong argued retort) from « il a une bonne punchline » (a strong quotable line) — juries expect the distinction.

blocks.heading: Les interrogatives à charge : inversion complexe et « n'est-ce pas que »
blocks.body: Debate questions are rarely neutral requests for information — they are built to corner. L'inversion complexe (Comment votre gouvernement peut-il expliquer…?) sounds formal and therefore harder to dismiss than a simple est-ce que. The tag n'est-ce pas que…? invites forced agreement by making disagreement sound unreasonable. Comment expliquer que + subjonctif presupposes the fact it questions — the subjunctive itself signals that the fact is treated as established, only its cause is up for debate.

examples.french: Comment votre gouvernement peut-il expliquer un tel retard ?
examples.english: How can your government explain such a delay?
examples.note: Inversion complexe: formal register, harder to deflect than « est-ce que ».

examples.french: N'est-ce pas vous qui promettiez, il y a quatre ans, le plein emploi ?
examples.english: Wasn't it you who promised, four years ago, full employment?
examples.note: The tag frames disagreement as denying an obvious fact.

examples.french: Comment expliquer que ce chiffre ait doublé en deux ans ?
examples.english: How is it to be explained that this figure doubled in two years?
examples.note: Subjonctif: the doubling is presupposed, only the cause is questioned.

examples.french: Peut-on sérieusement soutenir que rien n'a changé ?
examples.english: Can one seriously maintain that nothing has changed?

examples.french: Qu'avez-vous à répondre à ceux qui vous accusent d'immobilisme ?
examples.english: What do you have to say to those who accuse you of standing still?
examples.note: The accusation is voiced through a third party, protecting the moderator's neutrality.

examples.french: Une question à charge se reconnaît à ce qu'elle contient déjà sa propre réponse.
examples.english: A loaded question is recognisable by the fact that it already contains its own answer.

blocks.tip: Before answering a debate question, separate its presupposition from its actual content — many trap questions can be refused at the level of the presupposition alone.

blocks.heading: Concession et opposition à l'oral formel : certes… mais, cela dit, il n'empêche que
blocks.body: Live debate concession has to be fast: certes… mais grants a point and reverses it inside a single breath. Cela dit and il n'empêche que restart the sentence after a concession without sounding like a contradiction of oneself. Reserve néanmoins and quoi qu'il en soit for the more written-sounding, summarising moments — the closing statement rather than the rapid exchange — since their weight slows the rhythm the live format needs.

passages.title: Le débat d'entre-deux-tours (texte entièrement fictif)
passages.french:
Le débat d'entre-deux-tours, retransmis sur la Chaîne Nationale Valdonienne, a opposé Adrien Fabre à Camille Lorrain — un texte entièrement fictif, comme l'ensemble de cette leçon.
La modératrice, Sophie Ravenel, a ouvert la soirée en rappelant une règle simple : deux minutes trente par réponse, chronométrées sans exception.
Les premières minutes ont été feutrées, presque scolaires, chacun récitant son programme sans regarder l'autre.
Le premier vrai clash est arrivé sur la question des retraites, posée par Sophie Ravenel en inversion complexe : « Comment votre gouvernement peut-il justifier ce report ? »
Adrien Fabre a d'abord tenté de noyer le poisson, citant quatre réformes sans lien direct avec la question posée.
Camille Lorrain a coupé, presque en même temps que la modératrice : « Vous bottez en touche depuis une minute. »
La formule a fait rire le plateau, et Sophie Ravenel n'a pas rappelé sa contradictrice à l'ordre.
Fabre a repris la main en citant un chiffre unique — deux cent mille emplois créés — qu'aucun journaliste présent n'a pu vérifier en direct.
La réplique de Lorrain, mesurée, a suivi : « Certes, des emplois ont été créés, mais à quel salaire ? »
C'est là qu'est née la petite phrase de la soirée : « Des chiffres, pas des slogans », lancée par Lorrain avec un sourire calculé.
La punchline a circulé sur les réseaux avant même la fin du débat, coupée de tout contexte.
Sur l'immigration, la passe d'armes a duré près de dix minutes, chacun accusant l'autre d'invective.
Aucun des deux candidats n'a véritablement répondu à la question initiale de Sophie Ravenel.
Dans sa déclaration finale, Fabre a choisi le registre soutenu : « Néanmoins, je crois que les électeurs jugeront sur la durée. »
Lorrain, elle, a préféré une phrase courte, taillée pour le lendemain matin : « Ce soir, vous avez vu deux bilans ; à vous de choisir. »
Les instituts de sondage, interrogés dès la fin de l'émission, jugeaient l'échange nul, ce qui, en soi, disait déjà quelque chose du débat.
passages.english:
The run-off debate, broadcast on the Valdonian National Channel, pitted Adrien Fabre against Camille Lorrain — an entirely fictional text, like the whole of this lesson.
The moderator, Sophie Ravenel, opened the evening by recalling a simple rule: two and a half minutes per answer, timed without exception.
The first minutes were muted, almost schoolroom-like, each candidate reciting their platform without looking at the other.
The first real clash came on the pensions question, put by Sophie Ravenel using a complex inversion: "How can your government justify this delay?"
Adrien Fabre first tried to muddy the waters, citing four reforms with no direct link to the question asked.
Camille Lorrain cut in, almost at the same time as the moderator: "You've been dodging the question for a minute."
The line drew laughter from the set, and Sophie Ravenel did not call her fellow debater to order.
Fabre regained the initiative by citing a single figure — two hundred thousand jobs created — which no journalist present could verify live.
Lorrain's measured retort followed: "Granted, jobs have been created, but at what wage?"
That is where the soundbite of the evening was born: "Figures, not slogans", delivered by Lorrain with a calculated smile.
The punchline circulated online before the debate had even ended, stripped of all context.
On immigration, the sharp exchange lasted nearly ten minutes, each accusing the other of invective.
Neither candidate truly answered Sophie Ravenel's original question.
In his closing statement, Fabre chose the formal register: "Nevertheless, I believe the voters will judge over time."
Lorrain, for her part, preferred a short sentence, cut for the next morning's headlines: "Tonight, you saw two track records; the choice is yours."
The polling institutes, asked right after the programme ended, judged the exchange a draw, which, in itself, already said something about the debate.

lessons.title: La communication de crise politique
lessons.description: The technique of political crisis communication: containing a scandal in the media, controlling the narrative, and the syntax of controlled regret.

blocks.heading: Les premières heures : la cellule de crise et la mise au point
blocks.body: The first hours after a scandal breaks set the terms for everything after. Une cellule de crise assembles fast: the minister, the spokesperson, sometimes outside communication counsel. Its first product is usually la mise au point — a clarification, not yet an apology, meant to slow the story rather than end it. A mise au point differs from le communiqué (a routine statement) in stakes: it is issued specifically because the previous account has been challenged, and it must correct just enough to sound honest without conceding the whole story.

examples.french: Une cellule de crise a été réunie dès l'annonce des premières révélations.
examples.english: A crisis unit was assembled as soon as the first revelations broke.
examples.note: Invented scenario, built around the fictional minister Marc Delannoy.

examples.french: Le ministère a publié une mise au point avant même la fin de la journée.
examples.english: The ministry issued a clarification before the day was even over.

examples.french: Une mise au point corrige un détail ; elle ne reconnaît jamais l'ensemble du problème.
examples.english: A clarification corrects one detail; it never acknowledges the whole problem.

examples.french: Le communiqué initial ne mentionnait ni le montant ni les dates du marché contesté.
examples.english: The initial press release mentioned neither the amount nor the dates of the disputed contract.

examples.french: La vitesse de la réponse compte souvent plus que son contenu, dans les premières heures.
examples.english: In the first hours, the speed of the response often matters more than its content.

blocks.tip: Compare the timestamp of the first mise au point with the timestamp of the original story — a same-day response signals a prepared crisis plan, not an improvised one.

blocks.heading: Nier, minimiser, reconnaître : la gradation contrôlée
blocks.body: Crisis communication rarely moves straight to confession. It typically passes through a graded sequence: nier the facts outright, then minimiser their scale once denial becomes untenable, then reconnaître les faits — but usually only the facts that are already public, phrased so as to sound like transparency rather than defeat. Éluder and démentir often appear at the denial stage; l'aveu, when it finally comes, is nearly always partial and carefully timed to a moment of low media attention, such as a Friday evening.

examples.french: Le ministre a d'abord nié toute irrégularité dans l'attribution du marché.

examples.note: Stage one: outright denial.

blocks.heading: Reprendre le récit : redorer l'image, contenir les dégâts
blocks.body: Once the facts are acknowledged, the work shifts from denial to narrative control. Redorer son image does not undo the scandal; it builds a new, more favourable story alongside it. Contenir les dégâts (limiting the damage) and endiguer la polémique (stemming the controversy) describe the same defensive goal at different scales — the individual's reputation versus the wider media storm. Notice how much of the vocabulary is spatial: contenir, endiguer, se murer, as though the crisis were a flood to be managed rather than a fact to be resolved.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel passé et le regret contrôlé
blocks.body: Crisis French favours a specific tense for admitting fault without fully admitting it: le conditionnel passé. Nous aurions dû informer plus tôt states a should-have without stating why it did not happen or who is responsible. Nous regrettons que + subjonctif passé regrets an event as a completed, slightly abstract fact — grammatically similar to regretting the weather. Contrast this with the passé composé of direct admission (nous avons commis une erreur), which is rare precisely because it assigns clear responsibility.

examples.french: Nous aurions dû informer le public plus tôt.
examples.english: We should have informed the public sooner.
examples.note: Conditionnel passé: acknowledges a lapse without naming a cause or an author.

examples.french: Nous regrettons que cette situation ait pu créer une confusion.
examples.english: We regret that this situation may have created confusion.
examples.note: Subjonctif passé: the confusion is regretted as a fact, not owned as a consequence.

examples.french: On aurait pu communiquer différemment ; ce n'est pas ce qui a été fait.
examples.english: One could have communicated differently; that is not what was done.

blocks.tip: Count how many sentences in a crisis statement use the conditionnel passé versus the passé composé — the ratio tells you how much responsibility is actually being claimed.

blocks.heading: Atténuation syntaxique : dans la mesure où, sans vouloir minimiser, il convient de
blocks.body: Beyond vocabulary, crisis French hedges through subordinating structures. Dans la mesure où frames a statement as conditionally true rather than flatly true. Sans vouloir + infinitive disclaims an effect while producing exactly that effect (sans vouloir minimiser les faits often precedes a minimisation). Il convient de rappeler que reframes an inconvenient fact as a neutral, almost administrative reminder. These structures let a spokesperson stay grammatically correct and factually careful while giving away as little ground as possible.

passages.title: L'affaire des marchés de Bellerive (texte entièrement fictif)
passages.french:
L'affaire a commencé un lundi, quand La Gazette de Sormont a publié un article sur des marchés publics attribués dans la région de Bellerive — un texte entièrement fictif, comme l'ensemble de cette leçon.
Le ministre des Transports, Marc Delannoy, était directement mis en cause dans l'attribution de ces contrats.
Le ministère a réagi en moins de deux heures par un communiqué bref, qui démentait « toute irrégularité ».
Le lendemain, une cellule de crise s'est réunie dans les bureaux du ministère, portes closes.
Nadia Ferrand, porte-parole du ministère, a publié une première mise au point, sans reconnaître le montant exact des marchés en cause.
La rumeur d'une démission a couru toute la semaine, sans jamais être confirmée.
Marc Delannoy, lui, s'est muré dans le silence pendant près d'une semaine, refusant toute interview.
Le tollé, dans l'opposition comme dans certains médias, a fini par forcer une conférence de presse.
« Nous aurions dû informer le public plus tôt », a reconnu Nadia Ferrand, sans jamais préciser pourquoi cela n'avait pas été fait.
« Sans vouloir minimiser les faits, il faut resituer ce dossier dans son contexte », a-t-elle ajouté aussitôt.
Le ministère a ensuite tenté d'endiguer la polémique par l'annonce d'une enquête administrative interne.
Cette enquête, dans la mesure où elle était menée par le ministère lui-même, n'a convaincu ni l'opposition ni la presse.
L'éclaboussure a fini par atteindre deux autres élus de la région de Bellerive.
Marc Delannoy a présenté ses excuses dix jours après les premières révélations, un vendredi soir.
Il n'a pas démissionné, et sa cote de popularité, contre toute attente, n'a que légèrement baissé.
L'affaire illustre une règle simple de la communication de crise : contenir les dégâts compte souvent plus que résoudre le problème.
passages.english:
The affair began on a Monday, when the Sormont Gazette published an article on public contracts awarded in the Bellerive region — an entirely fictional text, like the whole of this lesson.
The Minister of Transport, Marc Delannoy, was directly implicated in the awarding of these contracts.
The ministry responded within two hours with a brief press release denying "any irregularity".
The next day, a crisis unit met behind closed doors at the ministry.
Nadia Ferrand, the ministry's spokesperson, issued a first clarification, without acknowledging the exact amount of the contracts in question.
Rumours of a resignation ran all week, never confirmed.
Marc Delannoy, for his part, went silent for nearly a week, refusing all interviews.
The outcry, from the opposition and from parts of the media, eventually forced a press conference.
"We should have informed the public sooner," Nadia Ferrand admitted, without ever specifying why that had not been done.
"Without wishing to downplay the facts, this matter needs to be put in context," she added immediately afterwards.
The ministry then tried to stem the controversy by announcing an internal administrative inquiry.
That inquiry, insofar as it was conducted by the ministry itself, convinced neither the opposition nor the press.
The fallout eventually reached two other elected officials from the Bellerive region.
Marc Delannoy offered his apology ten days after the first revelations, on a Friday evening.
He did not resign, and his approval rating, against all expectations, dropped only slightly.
The affair illustrates a simple rule of crisis communication: containing the damage often matters more than solving the problem.
